instructions.content: Identify SRP violations: list classes with more than one reason to change, such as business logic plus persistence plus notifications, and split them.
Check open-closed compliance: where new features require editing stable code, introduce abstraction or polymorphism.
Validate Liskov substitution: subtypes must preserve base contracts, not strengthen preconditions or weaken postconditions, and clients should not need type checks.
Segregate interfaces by client need so clients depend only on methods they use.
Invert dependencies: introduce abstractions at module boundaries so high-level modules do not depend on low-level concrete types.
Record each finding in the three-line format: violation, refactor, validation.
Where a subtype cannot honour the base contract by throwing, use a Result type instead.
Provide the concrete implementation through injection (container or constructor) rather than instantiating it in business logic.
NEVER apply SOLID as a mechanical checklist to every class; apply it where the design is causing pain.
NEVER create God Classes to avoid too many files.
NEVER confuse ISP with one method per interface; group cohesive role-specific method sets.
NEVER use deep inheritance to satisfy OCP when composition achieves the same result.
Do not use this skill for service or module boundaries (use clean-architecture), structural pattern choice (use design-patterns) or testing strategy (use testable-design).
Use text searches to find candidate violations: multiple concerns, type checks and concrete instantiation under src.
